item: Row J: each catalogue is parsed once per start-up, with the collector paused while it parses
summary: A boot parsed 18 documents of seven catalogue files in one lifespan call (29 on a plaintext launch, whose _serve block seeds once before the lifespan does): the seeder, the law seed and the curated-domain set of the qualification stamp each parsed the same text. (a) _load_safe_yaml (name and signature unchanged) now runs the parse inside a counted collector pause: first entrant disables only if it was on, last leaver re-enables, restored on every exit, left off if the process had it off, and the pause registers itself before it switches (R171). (b) _parsed_catalogue keeps one parse per sha256 of the TEXT (the file is still read each time, so an edit is never served stale) until forget_parsed_catalogues(), the last statement of _run_startup_upkeep, ends start-up and stops holding new ones (a later scrape-time or coverage read parses as before and does not re-grow the held tree). load_sources_from_yaml hands out a copy of each entry dict; the law catalogue reader deep-copies what it returns because it writes country and jurisdiction into the entries and load_legal_catalog marks and merges them. A test runs the whole seeding block and asserts every text was parsed once, the held tree equals a fresh parse afterwards (no reader wrote a nested value into it) and the sources rows equal what parsing every time writes. Measured: Export's clean re-run on `ee373ebed` (`keyword-export/catalogue-parse-remeasure-1430-2026-10-17/clean-rerun/CLEAN-REPORT.md` sections 1 and 2; plain store, median of 5, 4 shared vCPUs, nothing else running; the base is the head with the memo and the pause reverted, so the figures say what they buy, not what J3 bought): first install (the lifespan call) 8,741 ms to 6,519 ms (-25.4 %), steady boot 4,447 ms to 2,262 ms (-49.1 %), plaintext first launch 11,003 ms to 7,140 ms (-35.1 %), parses per boot 18 to 7 (29 to 7 on the first launch); the stored data is identical between the trees and max RSS is unchanged. Not measured: the encrypted boot, Windows, macOS, a cold disk, a store with articles, more cores. The `_serve` double seed (0.6 to 0.85 s once per plaintext data folder, after the memo) stays: an open item, not a ruling. Not covered: Windows and macOS, a PyYAML wheel without libyaml, a cold disk, the effect on a request served during a parse (inferred harmless: deferred collection only). The _serve block still seeds twice; that is a separate decision (signal handling before install_signal_handlers, log lines, guard tests).
